summary_paragraph: The patient, a male with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatitis C, esophageal varices, and chronic alcohol use, presented to the emergency department with complaints of chest pain and bright red blood per rectum. He was alert and not intoxicated during this admission. Initial evaluation showed a negative troponin, stable hemoglobin, and a guaiac-negative rectal exam. Serial cardiac enzymes ruled out myocardial infarction, and improvement in hematocrit suggested no active gastrointestinal bleeding. The chest pain was determined to be atypical and reproducible on examination, making a musculoskeletal origin likely. The rectal bleeding was attributed to known internal hemorrhoids. Pain was managed with tramadol and a lidocaine patch. The patient was counseled on the importance of outpatient follow-up, including discussion of a stress test with his primary care provider, and encouraged to reduce alcohol use. He was discharged home in stable condition with clear instructions and medications.
problems: Internal hemorrhoids without mention of complication
